recipes.title: Area between two curves (two crossings)
recipes.type: Find the area of the region enclosed between $y=\text{Expr}_1(x)$ and $y=\text{Expr}_2(x)$, where they meet at two points.

example.problem: Find the area of the region enclosed between $y=12-x^2$ and $y=x^2-6$.

steps.do: Find the points of intersection by solving $\text{Expr}_1(x)=\text{Expr}_2(x)$ for $x$. One root means the region is infinite (no finite answer). Two roots $x_1<x_2$ are your limits of integration. With three intersection points, split the interval at the middle one and add the two areas.
On each interval of integration (here just one), decide which curve is on top by plugging in a test value (or sketching).
steps.work: At $x=0$ the first curve gives $12$ and the second gives $-6$. Since $12>-6$: $\text{TOP}=12-x^2$, $\text{BOT}=x^2-6$.

steps.do: The area is $\displaystyle\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\big[\text{TOP}(x)-\text{BOT}(x)\big]\,dx$.

On each interval of integration (here just one), decide which curve is on top by plugging in a test value (or sketching).
steps.work: At $x=0$ the first curve gives $8$ and the second gives $0$. So $\text{TOP}=8-x^2$, $\text{BOT}=x^2$.

steps.do: The area is $\displaystyle\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\big[\text{TOP}(x)-\text{BOT}(x)\big]\,dx$.

On each interval of integration (here just one), decide which curve is on top by plugging in a test value (or sketching).
steps.work: At $x=0$ the first curve gives $0$ and the second gives $-2$. So $\text{TOP}=x$, $\text{BOT}=x^2-2$.

recipes.title: Area between two curves (three crossings)
recipes.type: Find the area of the region enclosed between $y=\text{Expr}_1(x)$ and $y=\text{Expr}_2(x)$, where they meet at three points.

example.problem: Find the area of the region enclosed between $y=x^3-x$ and $y=3x$.

steps.do: Find the points of intersection by solving $\text{Expr}_1(x)=\text{Expr}_2(x)$ for $x$. Three roots $x_1<x_2<x_3$ mean you need TWO integrals, one over $[x_1,x_2]$ and one over $[x_2,x_3]$.
On each interval of integration, decide which curve is on top by plugging in a test value (or sketching).
steps.work: On $(-2,0)$ test $x=-1$: $x^3-x$ gives $0$, $3x$ gives $-3$, so $\text{TOP}=x^3-x$, $\text{BOT}=3x$. On $(0,2)$ test $x=1$: $x^3-x$ gives $0$, $3x$ gives $3$, so $\text{TOP}=3x$, $\text{BOT}=x^3-x$.

steps.do: The area is the sum $\displaystyle\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\big[\text{TOP}-\text{BOT}\big]dx+\int_{x_2}^{x_3}\big[\text{TOP}-\text{BOT}\big]dx$. Usually who is TOP and who is BOT switches between the intervals.

steps.do: The area is the sum $\displaystyle\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\big[\text{TOP}-\text{BOT}\big]dx+\int_{x_2}^{x_3}\big[\text{TOP}-\text{BOT}\big]dx$. Usually who is TOP and who is BOT switches between the intervals.

recipes.title: Volume by disks about the x-axis
recipes.type: Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by $y=f(x)$, $x=a$, $x=b$, $y=0$ about the $x$-axis.

example.problem: Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by $y=1/x^2$, $x=1$, $x=2$, $y=0$ about the $x$-axis.

steps.do: Sketch the region and check that the bottom boundary is the $x$-axis ($y=0$). Then the volume is $\displaystyle V=\pi\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx$.
steps.work: Since $y=0$ (the $x$-axis) is one of the boundaries, the volume is simply $$V=\pi\int_1^2\Big(\frac1{x^2}\Big)^2dx$$

steps.do: Evaluate the integral.

recipes.title: Volume by washers about the x-axis
recipes.type: Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by $y=f(x)$ and $x=g(y)$ about the $x$-axis.

example.problem: Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by $y=x^2$ and $y^2=x$ about the $x$-axis.

steps.do: Sketch the two curves and find where they intersect. Decide who is TOP and who is BOTTOM, writing both as $y=\text{Expression}(x)$. The intersection $x$-values are your limits $a$ and $b$ (with more than two intersections, split the interval at each intersection).
steps.work: Solving $\{y^2=x,\ y=x^2\}$ gives $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$, so the limits are $x=0$ and $x=1$. TOP is the curve $x=y^2$, i.e. $y=\sqrt x$; BOTTOM is $y=x^2$.

steps.do: With limits $x=a$ and $x=b$, the volume is $\displaystyle V=\pi\int_a^b\big(\text{TOP}^2-\text{BOTTOM}^2\big)dx$.
Evaluate the integral.

practice.problem: Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by $y=x^2$ and $y=x$ about the $x$-axis. Enter the volume.

steps.do: Sketch the two curves and find where they intersect. Decide who is TOP and who is BOTTOM, writing both as $y=\text{Expression}(x)$. The intersection $x$-values are your limits $a$ and $b$ (with more than two intersections, split the interval at each intersection).
steps.work: Setting $x^2=x$ gives $x(x-1)=0$, so the limits are $x=0$ and $x=1$. At $x=\tfrac12$: $y=x$ gives $\tfrac12$, $y=x^2$ gives $\tfrac14$, so TOP $=x$ and BOTTOM $=x^2$.

steps.do: With limits $x=a$ and $x=b$, the volume is $\displaystyle V=\pi\int_a^b\big(\text{TOP}^2-\text{BOTTOM}^2\big)dx$.
Evaluate the integral.

practice.problem: Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by $y=x^2$ and $y^2=8x$ about the $x$-axis. Enter the volume.

steps.do: Sketch the two curves and find where they intersect. Decide who is TOP and who is BOTTOM, writing both as $y=\text{Expression}(x)$. The intersection $x$-values are your limits $a$ and $b$ (with more than two intersections, split the interval at each intersection).
steps.work: Solving $\{y^2=8x,\ y=x^2\}$: $x^4=8x$, so $x(x^3-8)=0$ and $x=0$ or $x=2$. The limits are $x=0$ and $x=2$. TOP is $y=\sqrt{8x}$ and BOTTOM is $y=x^2$ (at $x=1$: $\sqrt8\approx2.83>1$).

steps.do: With limits $x=a$ and $x=b$, the volume is $\displaystyle V=\pi\int_a^b\big(\text{TOP}^2-\text{BOTTOM}^2\big)dx$.
Evaluate the integral.

recipes.title: Volume about a horizontal line y = A
recipes.type: Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ about the line $y=A$.

example.problem: Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by $y=x^4$ and $y=1$ about $y=2$.

steps.do: Convert everything to the $x$-language (if necessary), getting two functions of $x$. Set them equal to find the limits of integration. Sketch the region and decide which curve is FARTHER from the axis $y=A$ and which is CLOSER.
steps.work: Setting $x^4=1$: $x^4-1=(x^2-1)(x^2+1)=(x-1)(x+1)(x^2+1)=0$, so $x=-1$ and $x=1$ are the limits. From the sketch, $y=x^4$ is FARTHER from the axis $y=2$ and $y=1$ is CLOSER.

steps.do: With limits $x=a$ and $x=b$, the volume is $\displaystyle V=\pi\int_a^b\big((\text{FAR}-A)^2-(\text{CLOSER}-A)^2\big)dx$.
Evaluate the integral.

steps.work: Setting $x^2=4$ gives $x=-2$ and $x=2$. The axis $y=5$ is above the region, so $y=x^2$ (lower) is FARTHER from it and $y=4$ is CLOSER.

steps.do: With limits $x=a$ and $x=b$, the volume is $\displaystyle V=\pi\int_a^b\big((\text{FAR}-A)^2-(\text{CLOSER}-A)^2\big)dx$.
Evaluate the integral.

recipes.title: Shells between two curves
recipes.type: Use cylindrical shells to find the volume generated by rotating the region bounded by $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ about the $y$-axis.

example.problem: Use cylindrical shells to find the volume generated by rotating the region bounded by $y=3+2x-x^2$ and $x+y=3$ about the $y$-axis.

steps.do: Sketch the two curves and find the region they bound. This time you must find the limits yourself by solving $f(x)=g(x)$ (expect two roots $a<b$). Convert implicit curves to $y=\text{Expression}(x)$. Decide who is TOP and who is BOTTOM.
steps.work: First convert the line to explicit form: $x+y=3$ becomes $y=3-x$. Solving $3+2x-x^2=3-x$ gives $x^2-3x=0$, i.e. $x(x-3)=0$, so $x=0$ and $x=3$. From the sketch, $\text{TOP}=3+2x-x^2$ and $\text{BOTTOM}=3-x$.

steps.do: Set up the integral: $\displaystyle V=2\pi\int_a^b x\,(\text{TOP}-\text{BOTTOM})\,dx$.
Evaluate the integral.

steps.do: Sketch the two curves and find the region they bound. This time you must find the limits yourself by solving $f(x)=g(x)$ (expect two roots $a<b$). Convert implicit curves to $y=\text{Expression}(x)$. Decide who is TOP and who is BOTTOM.
steps.work: Both curves are already explicit. Solving $2x=x^2$ gives $x(x-2)=0$, so $x=0$ and $x=2$. At $x=1$: $2x=2>1=x^2$, so $\text{TOP}=2x$ and $\text{BOTTOM}=x^2$.

steps.do: Set up the integral: $\displaystyle V=2\pi\int_a^b x\,(\text{TOP}-\text{BOTTOM})\,dx$.
Evaluate the integral.

practice.problem: Use cylindrical shells to find the volume generated by rotating the region bounded by $y=3x-x^2$ and $y=x^2-3x$ about the $y$-axis. Enter the volume.

steps.do: Sketch the two curves and find the region they bound. This time you must find the limits yourself by solving $f(x)=g(x)$ (expect two roots $a<b$). Convert implicit curves to $y=\text{Expression}(x)$. Decide who is TOP and who is BOTTOM.
steps.work: Solving $3x-x^2=x^2-3x$ gives $2x^2-6x=0$, i.e. $2x(x-3)=0$, so $x=0$ and $x=3$. At $x=1$: $3x-x^2=2$ and $x^2-3x=-2$, so $\text{TOP}=3x-x^2$ and $\text{BOTTOM}=x^2-3x$.

steps.do: Set up the integral: $\displaystyle V=2\pi\int_a^b x\,(\text{TOP}-\text{BOTTOM})\,dx$.
Evaluate the integral.

recipes.title: Work to stretch a spring
recipes.type: A spring has natural length $a$ meters. If an $F_0$-Newton force is required to keep it stretched to $b$ meters, how much work is needed to stretch it from $c$ meters to $d$ meters?

example.problem: A spring has natural length 20 cm. If a 25-Newton force is required to keep it stretched to 30 cm, how much work is needed to stretch it from 25 cm to 30 cm?

steps.do: Find Hooke's constant $k=\dfrac{F_0}{b-a}$ (force divided by the stretched length beyond the natural length). Convert everything to standard units (meters)! The force is $F=kx$, where $x$ is the length beyond natural length.
steps.work: The stretched length is $30-20=10$ cm $=0.1$ m, and the force is $25$ N, so $k=25/0.1=250$ and $F=250x$.

steps.do: Set up the integral for the work: $\displaystyle W=\int_{c-a}^{d-a}kx\,dx$.
Evaluate the integral.

practice.problem: A spring has natural length 10 cm. If a 40-Newton force is required to keep it stretched to 15 cm, how much work (in joules) is needed to stretch it from 12 cm to 16 cm? Enter the work.

steps.do: Find Hooke's constant $k=\dfrac{F_0}{b-a}$ (force divided by the stretched length beyond the natural length). Convert everything to standard units (meters)! The force is $F=kx$, where $x$ is the length beyond natural length.
steps.work: The stretched length is $15-10=5$ cm $=0.05$ m, and the force is $40$ N, so $k=40/0.05=800$ and $F=800x$.

steps.do: Set up the integral for the work: $\displaystyle W=\int_{c-a}^{d-a}kx\,dx$.
steps.work: Beyond natural length the limits are $12-10=2$ cm $=0.02$ m and $16-10=6$ cm $=0.06$ m: $$W=\int_{0.02}^{0.06}800x\,dx$$

steps.do: Evaluate the integral.

practice.problem: A spring has natural length 2 m. If a 30-Newton force is required to keep it stretched to 2.5 m, how much work (in joules) is needed to stretch it from 2.2 m to 3 m? Enter the work.

steps.do: Find Hooke's constant $k=\dfrac{F_0}{b-a}$ (force divided by the stretched length beyond the natural length). Convert everything to standard units (meters)! The force is $F=kx$, where $x$ is the length beyond natural length.
steps.work: The stretched length is $2.5-2=0.5$ m and the force is $30$ N, so $k=30/0.5=60$ and $F=60x$.

steps.do: Set up the integral for the work: $\displaystyle W=\int_{c-a}^{d-a}kx\,dx$.
steps.work: Beyond natural length the limits are $2.2-2=0.2$ m and $3-2=1$ m: $$W=\int_{0.2}^{1}60x\,dx$$

steps.do: Evaluate the integral.

recipes.title: Work to lift coal with a cable
recipes.type: A cable that weighs $a$ lb/ft is used to lift $B$ lb of coal up a mineshaft $C$ ft deep. Find the work done.

example.problem: A cable that weighs 2 lb/ft is used to lift 800 lb of coal up a mineshaft 500 ft deep. Find the work done.

recipes.title: Average value and the point c
recipes.type: Find the average value of a function $f(x)$ on the interval $[a,b]$, and find $c$ such that $f(c)=f_{\text{ave}}$.

example.problem: Find the average value of $f(x)=(x-2)^2$ on the interval $[1,4]$ and find $c$ such that $f(c)=f_{\text{ave}}$.

steps.do: Use the formula $\displaystyle f_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ and set up the integral.
Evaluate the integral.
Solve $f(c)=f_{\text{ave}}$ for $c$. Keep only solutions in $[a,b]$.
steps.work: Solve $(c-2)^2=1$: $c-2=\pm1$, so $c=3$ or $c=1$. Both lie in $[1,4]$.

practice.problem: Find the average value of $f(x)=(x+1)^2$ on the interval $[0,3]$ and find $c$ in $[0,3]$ such that $f(c)=f_{\text{ave}}$. Enter $c$.

steps.do: Use the formula $\displaystyle f_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ and set up the integral.
Evaluate the integral.
Solve $f(c)=f_{\text{ave}}$ for $c$. Keep only solutions in $[a,b]$.
steps.work: Solve $(c+1)^2=7$: $c+1=\pm\sqrt7$, so $c=-1+\sqrt7\approx1.65$ or $c=-1-\sqrt7\approx-3.65$. Only $c=\sqrt7-1$ lies in $[0,3]$.

recipes.title: Parts: x times a trig function
recipes.type: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\text{Something}(x)\cdot\text{SomethingElse}(x)\,dx$.

example.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx$.

steps.do: Start with a blank table ($u=\ ,\ u'=\ ,\ v=\ ,\ v'=\ $). Decide which factor is $u$; the other is $v'$. Pick $v'$ so that $v$ is easy to find; a rule of thumb is that $x$ or a power of $x$ is usually (not always!) $u$.
Complete the table: differentiate $u$ to get $u'$, and integrate $v'$ to get $v$ (ignore the constant of integration).
Plug into $\int u\,v'\,dx=uv-\int u'v\,dx$ and evaluate the integral on the right. Add $+C$ at the very end.
steps.work: $$\int x\cos x\,dx=x\sin x-\int1\cdot\sin x\,dx=x\sin x+\cos x+C$$

recipes.type: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\text{Something}(x)\cdot\text{SomethingElse}(x)\,dx$, where a higher power of $x$ requires integrating by parts more than once.

example.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int x^3e^x\,dx$.

steps.do: Start with a blank table. Decide which factor is $u$ and which is $v'$ (pick $v'$ so $v$ is easy to find). A power of $x$ is often, but not always, $u$.
Complete the table: $u'$ by differentiating $u$, $v$ by integrating $v'$ (no constant).
Plug into $\int u\,v'\,dx=uv-\int u'v\,dx$.
The new integral is a little easier but often not immediate. Do it by parts again (and again, if needed), then retrace your steps. Add $+C$ at the very end.
steps.work: By parts on $\int x^2e^x\,dx$ ($u=x^2$, $v'=e^x$): $\int x^2e^x\,dx=x^2e^x-2\int xe^x\,dx$. One last time: $\int xe^x\,dx=(x-1)e^x$. Retracing, $$\int x^2e^x\,dx=(x^2-2x+2)e^x,\qquad\int x^3e^x\,dx=x^3e^x-3(x^2-2x+2)e^x=(x^3-3x^2+6x-6)e^x+C$$

example.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\sin^3x\,dx$.

steps.do: Split off one factor: write $\sin^{2n+1}x\,dx$ as $(\sin^2x)^n(\sin x\,dx)$, or $\cos^{2n+1}x\,dx$ as $(\cos^2x)^n(\cos x\,dx)$. Get ready to substitute $u=$ the OTHER function ($u=\cos x$ for sine, $u=\sin x$ for cosine).

recipes.title: Trig substitution for square roots

example.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$.

steps.do: If $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ shows up, substitute $x=a\sin\theta$ and use $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$. If $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ shows up, use $x=a\tan\theta$ and $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$. If $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$ shows up, use $x=a\sec\theta$ and $\sec^2\theta-1=\tan^2\theta$. You get a trig integral of the kind covered under Trigonometric Integrals.
Use the trigonometric-integral techniques to evaluate this trig integral.
Convert the answer back to the $x$-language (draw a right triangle, or use $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$).

practice.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx$. Enter an antiderivative.

steps.do: If $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ shows up, substitute $x=a\sin\theta$ and use $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$. If $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ shows up, use $x=a\tan\theta$ and $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$. If $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$ shows up, use $x=a\sec\theta$ and $\sec^2\theta-1=\tan^2\theta$. You get a trig integral of the kind covered under Trigonometric Integrals.
Use the trigonometric-integral techniques to evaluate this trig integral.
Convert the answer back to the $x$-language (draw a right triangle, or use $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$).
steps.work: Since $\sin\theta=\frac x2$: $\theta=\sin^{-1}\frac x2$ and $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta=2\cdot\frac x2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2}=\frac{x\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2}$. Hence $$\int\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx=2\sin^{-1}\frac x2+\frac{x\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2}+C$$

practice.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(1+x^2)^{3/2}}$. Enter an antiderivative.

steps.do: If $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ shows up, substitute $x=a\sin\theta$ and use $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$. If $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ shows up, use $x=a\tan\theta$ and $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$. If $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$ shows up, use $x=a\sec\theta$ and $\sec^2\theta-1=\tan^2\theta$. You get a trig integral of the kind covered under Trigonometric Integrals.
Use the trigonometric-integral techniques to evaluate this trig integral.
Convert the answer back to the $x$-language (draw a right triangle, or use $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$).
steps.work: Since $\tan\theta=x$, the right triangle has opposite side $x$, adjacent side $1$ and hypotenuse $\sqrt{1+x^2}$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$. Hence $$\int\frac{dx}{(1+x^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}+C$$

recipes.title: Partial fractions: two distinct factors
recipes.type: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{C_1x+C_2}{(x-a)(x-b)}\,dx$, where $a,b,C_1,C_2$ are numbers.

example.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{x-1}{(x-2)(x-3)}\,dx$.

steps.do: Express the integrand using partial fractions: $\text{Integrand}=\dfrac{A}{x-a}+\dfrac{B}{x-b}$, with $A$ and $B$ numbers to be determined.
Multiply both sides by the denominator, then plug in convenient values of $x$ (namely $x=a$ and $x=b$) to find $A$ and $B$. Put them back into the expression for the integrand.
steps.work: $x-1=A(x-3)+B(x-2)$. Plugging in $x=3$: $2=B\cdot1$, so $B=2$. Plugging in $x=2$: $1=A\cdot(-1)$, so $A=-1$. Hence $$\frac{x-1}{(x-2)(x-3)}=\frac{-1}{x-2}+\frac{2}{x-3}$$

steps.do: Integrate each piece separately using $\int\frac{dx}{x-c}=\ln|x-c|$. Add $+C$ at the very end.

recipes.title: Partial fractions: a repeated factor
recipes.type: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{C_1x^2+C_2x+C_3}{(x-a)(x-b)^2}\,dx$, where $a,b,C_1,C_2,C_3$ are numbers.

example.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2}{(x-3)(x+2)^2}\,dx$.

steps.do: Express the integrand using partial fractions: $\text{Integrand}=\dfrac{A}{x-a}+\dfrac{B}{x-b}+\dfrac{C}{(x-b)^2}$, with $A,B,C$ numbers to be determined.
Multiply both sides by the denominator and plug in convenient values of $x$ to get $A$ and $C$. To get $B$, equate the $x^2$ coefficients on both sides. Put the values back into the integrand.
steps.work: $x^2=A(x+2)^2+B(x-3)(x+2)+C(x-3)$. Plugging in $x=3$: $9=25A$, so $A=\frac{9}{25}$. Plugging in $x=-2$: $4=-5C$, so $C=-\frac45$. The $x^2$ coefficient is $1$ on the left and $A+B$ on the right, so $B=1-\frac{9}{25}=\frac{16}{25}$. Hence $$\frac{x^2}{(x-3)(x+2)^2}=\frac{9/25}{x-3}+\frac{16/25}{x+2}+\frac{-4/5}{(x+2)^2}$$

steps.do: Integrate each piece separately using $\int\frac{dx}{x-c}=\ln|x-c|$ and $\int\frac{dx}{(x-c)^2}=-\frac{1}{x-c}$. Add $+C$ at the very end.

recipes.title: Partial fractions: an irreducible quadratic
recipes.type: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{C_1x^2+C_2x+C_3}{(x-a)(x^2+b^2)}\,dx$, where $a,b,C_1,C_2,C_3$ are numbers.

example.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{10}{(x-1)(x^2+9)}\,dx$.

steps.do: Express the integrand using partial fractions: $\text{Integrand}=\dfrac{A}{x-a}+\dfrac{Bx+C}{x^2+b^2}$, with $A,B,C$ numbers to be determined.

Multiply both sides by the denominator and plug in the convenient value $x=a$ to get $A$ (the only real convenient value). Then equate coefficients to get two equations for $B$ and $C$. Put the values back into the integrand.
steps.work: $10=A(x^2+9)+(Bx+C)(x-1)=(A+B)x^2+(C-B)x+(9A-C)$. Plugging in $x=1$: $10=10A$, so $A=1$. Comparing the coefficients of $x^2$ and $x$: $0=A+B$ and $0=C-B$, so $B=-1$ and $C=-1$. Hence $$\frac{10}{(x-1)(x^2+9)}=\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{-x-1}{x^2+9}$$

steps.do: Integrate each piece separately using $\int\frac{dx}{x-c}=\ln|x-c|$, $\int\frac{2x\,dx}{x^2+b^2}=\ln(x^2+b^2)$ and $\int\frac{dx}{x^2+b^2}=\frac1b\tan^{-1}\frac xb$. Add $+C$ at the end.

steps.do: Express the integrand using partial fractions: $\text{Integrand}=\dfrac{A}{x-a}+\dfrac{Bx+C}{x^2+b^2}$, with $A,B,C$ numbers to be determined.

Multiply both sides by the denominator and plug in the convenient value $x=a$ to get $A$ (the only real convenient value). Then equate coefficients to get two equations for $B$ and $C$. Put the values back into the integrand.
steps.work: $3x^2+2x+5=A(x^2+4)+(Bx+C)(x-1)=(A+B)x^2+(C-B)x+(4A-C)$. Plugging in $x=1$: $10=5A$, so $A=2$. Comparing coefficients of $x^2$ and $x$: $3=A+B$ and $2=C-B$, so $B=1$ and $C=3$. Hence $$\frac{3x^2+2x+5}{(x-1)(x^2+4)}=\frac{2}{x-1}+\frac{x+3}{x^2+4}$$

steps.do: Integrate each piece separately using $\int\frac{dx}{x-c}=\ln|x-c|$, $\int\frac{2x\,dx}{x^2+b^2}=\ln(x^2+b^2)$ and $\int\frac{dx}{x^2+b^2}=\frac1b\tan^{-1}\frac xb$. Add $+C$ at the end.

practice.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{3x^2+x}{(x+1)(x^2+1)}\,dx$. Enter an antiderivative.

steps.do: Express the integrand using partial fractions: $\text{Integrand}=\dfrac{A}{x-a}+\dfrac{Bx+C}{x^2+b^2}$, with $A,B,C$ numbers to be determined.

Multiply both sides by the denominator and plug in the convenient value $x=a$ to get $A$ (the only real convenient value). Then equate coefficients to get two equations for $B$ and $C$. Put the values back into the integrand.
steps.work: $3x^2+x=A(x^2+1)+(Bx+C)(x+1)=(A+B)x^2+(B+C)x+(A+C)$. Plugging in $x=-1$: $2=2A$, so $A=1$. Comparing the coefficients of $x^2$ and the constant term: $3=A+B$ and $0=A+C$, so $B=2$ and $C=-1$ (check: $B+C=1$ ✓). Hence $$\frac{3x^2+x}{(x+1)(x^2+1)}=\frac{1}{x+1}+\frac{2x-1}{x^2+1}$$

recipes.title: Trapezoid, Midpoint and Simpson's Rules
recipes.type: Use (a) the Trapezoid Rule, (b) the Midpoint Rule and (c) Simpson's Rule to approximate $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ with the specified even integer $n$.

example.problem: Use (a) the Trapezoid Rule, (b) the Midpoint Rule and (c) Simpson's Rule to approximate $\displaystyle\int_2^6\frac1x\,dx$ with $n=8$.

steps.do: Find $\Delta x=\dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and list $x_0=a,\ x_1=a+\Delta x,\ \dots,\ x_n=b$. For the Midpoint Rule you also need the midpoints $\bar x_i$ of $[x_{i-1},x_i]$.

Apply the rules: $M_n=\Delta x\,[f(\bar x_1)+\cdots+f(\bar x_n)]$; $T_n=\frac{\Delta x}{2}[f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+\cdots+2f(x_{n-1})+f(x_n)]$; $S_n=\frac{\Delta x}{3}[f(x_0)+4f(x_1)+2f(x_2)+4f(x_3)+\cdots+2f(x_{n-2})+4f(x_{n-1})+f(x_n)]$ ($n$ must be even for Simpson).

recipes.title: Infinite limit of integration
recipes.type: Determine whether $\displaystyle\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$ is convergent or divergent, and evaluate it if it is convergent, where $f(x)$ is 'easy' to integrate.

example.problem: Determine whether $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{(4x+1)^2}\,dx$ is convergent or divergent. Evaluate it if it is convergent.

steps.do: Replace the $\infty$ by $R$ and evaluate $\displaystyle\int_a^R f(x)\,dx$, pretending $R$ is a number.
You get an expression in $R$. Take the limit as $R\to\infty$ (L'Hôpital if you like). If the limit exists, the integral converges to that value; otherwise (infinity or oscillation) it diverges.

example.answer: The improper integral converges and equals $\dfrac1{20}$.

recipes.title: Integrand blows up: convergent
recipes.type: Determine whether $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is convergent or divergent, and evaluate it if it is convergent, where $f(x)$ 'blows up' at $x=a$, at $x=b$, or at both.

example.problem: Determine whether $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{1}{\sqrt x}\,dx$ is convergent or divergent. Evaluate it if it is convergent.

steps.do: Decide which end the integrand blows up at (if both, split into two integrals). Replace the bad endpoint by $t$ and evaluate the integral, pretending $t$ is a number: e.g. $\displaystyle\int_t^b f(x)\,dx$ if it blows up at $x=a$.
steps.work: The integrand blows up at $x=0$. $$\int_t^1x^{-1/2}\,dx=\Big[\frac{x^{1/2}}{1/2}\Big]_t^1=\Big[2\sqrt x\Big]_t^1=2(1-\sqrt t)$$

steps.do: You get an expression in $t$. Take the limit (from the right if the bad point is $a$, from the left if it is $b$). If the limit exists, the integral converges to that value; otherwise it diverges.

example.answer: The improper integral converges and equals $2$.

steps.do: Decide which end the integrand blows up at (if both, split into two integrals). Replace the bad endpoint by $t$ and evaluate the integral, pretending $t$ is a number: e.g. $\displaystyle\int_t^b f(x)\,dx$ if it blows up at $x=a$.
You get an expression in $t$. Take the limit (from the right if the bad point is $a$, from the left if it is $b$). If the limit exists, the integral converges to that value; otherwise it diverges.

practice.answer: The improper integral converges and equals $6$.

practice.problem: Determine whether $\displaystyle\int_1^3\frac{1}{\sqrt{3-x}}\,dx$ is convergent or divergent. If it converges, enter its value.

steps.do: Decide which end the integrand blows up at (if both, split into two integrals). Replace the bad endpoint by $t$ and evaluate the integral, pretending $t$ is a number: e.g. $\displaystyle\int_t^b f(x)\,dx$ if it blows up at $x=a$.
steps.work: The integrand blows up at $x=3$ (the upper end), so replace $3$ by $t$: $$\int_1^t(3-x)^{-1/2}\,dx=\Big[-2\sqrt{3-x}\Big]_1^t=-2\sqrt{3-t}+2\sqrt2$$

steps.do: You get an expression in $t$. Take the limit (from the right if the bad point is $a$, from the left if it is $b$). If the limit exists, the integral converges to that value; otherwise it diverges.

practice.answer: The improper integral converges and equals $2\sqrt2$.

recipes.title: Comparison theorem
recipes.type: Use the comparison theorem to determine whether $\displaystyle\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$ is convergent or divergent.

example.problem: Determine whether $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty\frac{\cos^2x}{1+x^2}\,dx$ is convergent or divergent. Do not evaluate!

steps.do: Decide on an 'easy' integrand to compare with, hoping the rest is bounded by a number. Check whether the easy integral converges (or diverges).
steps.work: $\frac{\cos^2x}{1+x^2}$ is 'similar' to $\frac1{1+x^2}$, which we know (or can find out) is convergent: $$\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\Big[\tan^{-1}x\Big]_1^\infty=\frac\pi2-\frac\pi4=\frac\pi4$$

steps.do: Look at the leftover factor and bound it. If $0\le f\le$ (a convergent integrand), the integral converges. If $f\ge$ (a divergent integrand)$\ge0$, it diverges.
steps.work: Since $\cos x$ is always between $-1$ and $1$, $\cos^2x\le1$, so $\dfrac{\cos^2x}{1+x^2}\le\dfrac1{1+x^2}$ and $$\int_1^\infty\frac{\cos^2x}{1+x^2}\,dx\le\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{1+x^2}<\infty$$ so the integral converges.

practice.problem: Use the comparison theorem to determine whether $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty\frac{\sin^2x}{x^2}\,dx$ is convergent or divergent. Enter \"converges\" or \"diverges\".

steps.do: Decide on an 'easy' integrand to compare with, hoping the rest is bounded by a number. Check whether the easy integral converges (or diverges).
Look at the leftover factor and bound it. If $0\le f\le$ (a convergent integrand), the integral converges. If $f\ge$ (a divergent integrand)$\ge0$, it diverges.
steps.work: Since $\sin^2x\le1$, $\dfrac{\sin^2x}{x^2}\le\dfrac1{x^2}$ and $$\int_1^\infty\frac{\sin^2x}{x^2}\,dx\le\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2}=1<\infty$$ so the integral converges.

practice.problem: Use the comparison theorem to determine whether $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty\frac{2+\cos x}{x}\,dx$ is convergent or divergent. Enter \"converges\" or \"diverges\".

steps.do: Decide on an 'easy' integrand to compare with, hoping the rest is bounded by a number. Check whether the easy integral converges (or diverges).
steps.work: $\frac{2+\cos x}{x}$ is 'similar' to $\frac1x$, which is divergent: $$\int_1^R\frac{dx}{x}=\ln R\to\infty\quad(R\to\infty)$$

steps.do: Look at the leftover factor and bound it. If $0\le f\le$ (a convergent integrand), the integral converges. If $f\ge$ (a divergent integrand)$\ge0$, it diverges.
steps.work: Since $\cos x\ge-1$, $2+\cos x\ge1$, so $\dfrac{2+\cos x}{x}\ge\dfrac1x$ and $$\int_1^\infty\frac{2+\cos x}{x}\,dx\ge\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x}=\infty$$ so the integral diverges.

recipes.title: Length of a curve y = f(x)

example.problem: Find the length of the curve $y=\ln(\cos x)$, $0\le x\le\pi/3$.

steps.do: Find the derivative $f'(x)$.
Set up the definite integral $\displaystyle L=\int_a^b\sqrt{1+f'(x)^2}\,dx$.
Evaluate the integral.
steps.work: From the table of integrals, $\int\sec x\,dx=\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C$, so $$L=\Big[\ln|\sec x+\tan x|\Big]_0^{\pi/3}=\ln(2+\sqrt3)-\ln(1+0)=\ln(2+\sqrt3)$$
